note: Batch 3 of the complexity audit — the opinionated tier, user-selected. 3a: nestor ui's fleet-gate integration is opt-in (no startup probe of a hardcoded willow governance path; activates only on --gate-rollup/NESTOR_GATE_ROLLUP). 3b (governance, at the user's 'friction only, gates intact' depth): the review-desk write-gate is surfaced at SessionStart so it is never a cold block, and the doubled before_authority hook subprocess is collapsed into before_write/before_bash (one process per tool call) with two new hook_guard cases proving authority still denies on the wired paths. 3c (three behaviour-preserving refactors, each done by a Sonnet agent, each verified by the full suite at 1417): memory.add_pair 270->~50 lines over 8 named helpers; portable.import_bundle 270->~157 over 6 helpers; the nine capability checks consolidated into one storage.py registry (supports/require_capability). A finding surfaced: the authority tripwire substring-matches minting phrases in any Bash command, so a git commit whose message merely describes them trips it.

decisions.question: The nestor ui probed a hardcoded willow governance rollup path at startup and lit fleet widgets for everyone. Keep the default-on convenience for the fleet deployment, or make it opt-in?
decisions.commitment: Opt-in. The startup auto-probe is removed; the fleet-gate echo activates only when --gate-rollup or NESTOR_GATE_ROLLUP names a rollup. With neither set the echo returns no entries and the widgets (already behind the fleet-gap domain filter) stay dormant. The --gate-rollup help drops the org vocabulary and the default-on claim.
decisions.why: A domain-agnostic verification UI reaching outside its own directory to a hardcoded, dated path in one operator's home is one deployment's workflow leaking into the general product — the same fleet-bleed the audit flagged, and a contradiction of the README's 'no upward dependency on any host'. Opt-in keeps the integration fully available to the fleet operator who wants it while a plain install sees nothing willow-shaped.
decisions.doors_closed: A general product probing a hardcoded external path at startup (reaches outside its directory unasked; ties the default UI to one org's file layout).

decisions.question: Collapsing the doubled hook subprocess means editing the live session's own enforcement wiring. How is 'gates intact' guaranteed rather than asserted?
decisions.commitment: The authority tripwire is run INSIDE the before_write/before_bash dispatch (first-to-block wins, authority first) and its standalone PreToolUse block is removed — one process instead of two. The collapse is behaviour-preserving by construction (same evaluators, same fail-open-on-own-bug), and it is PROVEN, not assumed: two new hook_guard cases assert the wired write and bash paths still deny a keyring write and a key-minting command via authority, and they were run green before the settings.json edit was trusted; a live check confirmed the wired path still blocks.
decisions.why: Enforcement wiring is exactly where a latency tidy-up can silently fail open, so the bar for touching it is a proof, not a claim. hook_guard drives the real wrapper at the wire level, so a case that denies there proves the gate the runtime will actually hit. Proving before trusting — and keeping the standalone before_authority module and its own cases for the unit proof — means the collapse cannot have dropped the tripwire without a red test.
decisions.doors_closed: A subprocess collapse that removes a gate from the wired path without a wire-level proof it still fires (fail-open enforcement, undetected).

decisions.question: The three core refactors touch the seal/conflict/trust hot paths. How is 'behaviour-preserving' enforced when the whole point is to move 270-line functions around?
decisions.commitment: Each refactor is a pure extract-method: every exception type and message, every guard condition and branch order, every ledger write, warning, report key, and the id-remap/no-dangling and race-retry invariants stay byte-identical — only relocated into named helpers. Each was run against the full suite (1417 passed, the import-trust and capability tests included) as the behaviour-preservation proof, and its diff reviewed to confirm the raises/warnings/report-keys were relocated, not edited. A capability's bespoke require that did not fit the registry table was left inline rather than forced.
decisions.why: On a hot path the test suite is the contract: a green full run over well-covered seal/import/capability logic is the evidence that packaging changed and behaviour did not. Reviewing the diff for moved-not-edited raises guards against a refactor that quietly changes a message or a condition the suite happens not to pin. Leaving the bespoke pieces inline keeps the refactor honest — a partial consolidation that is correct beats a total one that risks the trust boundary.
decisions.doors_closed: Forcing every case into a uniform helper at the cost of a changed exception, message, or trust decision on the seal/import path.
